title: Climate change contributed to Nepal rock-ice avalanche: scientists - everestchronicle.com
description: Climate change contributed to Nepal rock-ice avalanche: scientists  everestchronicle.com
publisher.title: everestchronicle.com
full_article:
A catastrophic rock-and-ice avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal's border with China last month was made more likely by global warming, which weakened glaciers and mountain permafrost, an international team of scientists said Thursday.

The assessment, one of the first comprehensive scientific studies of the August 26 catastrophe, found that climate change was a destabilising factor acting on a mountain slope already vulnerable because of its underlying geology.

The disaster began when about two square kilometres of rock wall and glacier ice collapsed from Langtang Lirung at an altitude of about 5,150 metres.

The collapsing mass plunged roughly 1,400 metres to the valley floor, releasing energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.5 earthquake and producing seismic waves initially detected as an earthquake-like signal.

The avalanche rapidly transformed into a debris flood, carrying rock, ice, sediment and water down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.

The torrent reached the Rasuwagadhi border, about 22 kilometres downstream, in seven minutes, travelling at an average speed of 188 kilometres per hour, the researchers said.

It then swept through Timure and Syabrubesi before reaching the Trishuli valley and devastating communities including Betrawati and Trishuli Bazaar.

The flood travelled about 200 kilometres to Devghat in less than seven hours, where river discharge more than doubled to about 5,850 cubic metres per second. Around 30.5 million cubic metres of sediment and debris were deposited along the disaster corridor.

Nepal's disaster authorities had recorded more than 1,300 deaths and more than 5,000 people missing by September 14, while thousands more had been rescued or treated.

The international team included researchers from Nepal, Pakistan, Britain, Ireland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, the United States, New Zealand and the Netherlands, with expertise ranging from glaciology and mountain hydrology to climate science and seismology.

The scientists said the geological structure ultimately controlled where and how the slope failed, while several factors may have contributed to its instability.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015 triggered another major rock-and-ice avalanche in the Langtang region and may have weakened the mountain's underlying rock mass over the longer term, although its specific contribution to the 2026 collapse could not yet be established.

The researchers also identified warming temperatures, permafrost degradation, glacier thinning and changing precipitation patterns as potential contributing factors.

Glaciers in the region have been losing more than half a metre in thickness each year, while the retreat of the Langtang-Lirung glacier has accelerated since 2010.

The freezing level has also risen by about 100 metres per decade in recent decades during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons, increasing the potential for permafrost thaw and glacier loss.

July and August 2026 were unusually warm around the disaster site. The researchers found that human-caused climate change had increased temperatures during those months by about 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with a climate 1.4C cooler than today.

But the scientists stressed that they had not determined whether the avalanche would have occurred without human-caused climate change.

Instead, they said climate change should be understood as a factor that can increase instability in already vulnerable mountain terrain.

The assessment also concluded that the disaster was beyond the design and predictive limits of existing warning systems, highlighting the difficulty of protecting communities from extremely rapid and cascading mountain hazards.

It called for stronger high-altitude monitoring, earth observation, risk communication and data sharing between countries, alongside greater support for communities facing climate-related loss and damage.

title: Nepal flash flood death toll surges to 1,410; over 6,100 still missing - The Hindu
description: Nepal flash flood death toll surges to 1,410; over 6,100 still missing  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal surged to 1,410 on Thursday (September 17, 2026), with over 6,100 people still missing, according to the country's disaster management authorities.

Flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

India approves expedited export of electricity to flood-hit Nepal

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

According to the data issued by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority(NDRRMA) on Thursday evening, 1,410 people have been killed in the floods so far, with 6,145 people still missing.

According to NDRRMA, 364 dead bodies have been recovered from Chitwan district, 232 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West, and 203 from Nuwakot.

Similarly, 199 bodies have been recovered from Rasuwa, 78 bodies from Gorkha, 72 bodies from Dhading and 38 bodies from Tanahu.

Two flood victims died in Kathmandu hospitals while undergoing treatment.

So far, 13,756 people have been rescued from the flood-affected areas.

The joint command of security personnel continues to carry out search and rescue operations in the flood-affected areas.

title: UC Davis dean, professor among thousands missing after Nepal-Tibet flood - The California Aggie
description: UC Davis dean, professor among thousands missing after Nepal-Tibet flood  The California Aggie
publisher.title: The California Aggie
full_article:
Married couple Rao and Vasu Unnava have not been heard from since the Aug. 26 flash flood

By KIMBERLY AYSON — campus@theaggie.org

Two married UC Davis faculty members are among the thousands still missing after last month’s Nepal-Tibet flash flood.

Husband and wife Rao and Vasu Unnava joined UC Davis in June 2016, when Rao was appointed dean of the UC Davis Graduate School of Management. That year, Vasu became an adjunct associate professor teaching marketing and studying consumer behavior.

On July 1, Rao stepped down as dean to go on sabbatical leave for a year and work with the Innovation Institute for Food and Health, according to the university . He was scheduled to return to the Graduate School of Management in 2027 as a professor of marketing. His retirement as dean was celebrated by a trip to Mount Kailash on the border of China, after which the pair planned to spend two months with family in India.

On Aug. 26, the Unnavas were staying at Hotel Kailash in Timure, Nepal, when a flash flood powered through the China-Nepal border, burying and destroying infrastructure — including the hotel.

The Unnavas have yet to be heard from or located since the floods. Search efforts to find the couple and others missing in the disaster remain underway.

The flash flood is speculated to have been caused by chunks of falling glacial ice and rock debris near the Himalayas into nearby rivers, according to the United States Geological Survey . The fallout of ice and rock, equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, sent surges of water downstream for a 62-mile stretch along the Himalayan border region of Nepal and Tibet.

The flash flood has claimed more than 1,300 lives and around 5,000 individuals are still missing as of Sept. 9, according to Nepalese authorities.

A statement released by Chancellor Gary May and Provost Mary Croughan on Sept. 3 assured the UC Davis community that the university’s global risk management, security and crisis response contractor is currently working with local authorities in Nepal and the U.S. Department of State to search for the Unnavas.

The statement notes that the Unnavas’ children and extended family have requested assistance from U.S. government agencies to find the couple.

“We continue to hope Rao and Vasu will be found safe and sound,” the statement reads. “Again, please keep them, their children, and extended family in your thoughts and prayers.”

Before working at UC Davis, the Unnavas taught at the Ohio State University’s (OSU) Fisher College of Business as professors of marketing. There, Rao also served as the associate dean of undergraduate programs, associate dean of executive education and director of doctoral programs in business. He worked at OSU for 32 years until his departure in 2016.

Rao’s tenure as dean of the UC Davis Graduate School of Management saw the launch of the first online Master of Business Administration program in the UC system and a new undergraduate business major, which welcomed its first cohort of students in fall 2025.

Tom Smith, dean of the UC Davis School of Education, has served as interim dean of the Graduate School of Management since July. The university says he will lead both schools until the appointment of a permanent dean, which Croughan said in a June announcement could happen as early as 2027.

For those seeking mental health and wellness support, UC Davis community members can contact the Academic and Staff Assistance Program or Student Health and Counseling Services .

title: Want to help Nepal recover from its deadly floods? Here’s what tourists need to know - UQ News
description: Want to help Nepal recover from its deadly floods? Here’s what tourists need to know  UQ News
publisher.title: UQ News
full_article:
The catastrophic floods that struck Nepal and Tibet in late August caused widespread destruction and enormous loss of life, killing at least 1,386 people, with thousands more still missing.

The immediate priority since then has rightly been rescue, relief and restoring essential services.

But ever since the deadly floods, Nepal has been appealing to international tourists not to cancel their travel plans. Much of the country is still open to visitors. Without tourism, what has been a disaster for parts of the country will end up hurting communities across the nation.

For a country so dependent on tourism, one of the hardest questions is now when, and how, to encourage visitors to come back.

1 in 7 jobs rely on tourism

Almost 1.16 million foreign tourists visited Nepal last year, its best year since before the COVID pandemic.

Tourism supports about 15% of Nepal’s employment – almost one job in seven – and its benefits reach from hotels and trekking companies to guides, porters, restaurants, transport operators and remote communities. The industry contributes about 6–8% of Nepal’s gross domestic product.

But past disasters in Nepal and elsewhere show that getting tourism recovery right can be surprisingly difficult.

Encourage visitors back too soon and they can impede recovery. Wait too long, and communities that depend on tourism can suffer a second, economic crisis.

The danger is that the economic footprint of this disaster could spread to have an even wider national impact than the floods themselves.

Lessons from past disasters

Tourists respond not only to actual risk, but to what they believe the risk to be. Media coverage, social media and travel advice all shape those perceptions.

For distant travellers, “disaster in Nepal” can quickly become a false impression that “all of Nepal is unsafe”.

This creates what we might call a “perception footprint”, which can be considerably larger than the area physically affected.

Nepal experienced this after the 2015 Gorkha earthquakes, which killed more than 8,800 people.

International arrivals fell 32% in 2015 compared to the year before, even though major destinations including Pokhara in the Himalayas and Chitwan were not directly affected.

Images of damaged temples, buildings and communities nevertheless contributed to a much broader perception of a devastated country.

Nepal eventually recovered strongly. Visitor numbers began growing again in 2016 and rose to a then record of 940,000 in 2017.

Tourism authorities used international media, partnerships and tourists’ social media posts to demonstrate that people were safely returning to many parts of the country.

The same challenges have occurred in other tourism destinations impacted by natural disasters.

The 2011 Queensland floods in Australia claimed 33 lives and caused widespread damage across an area the size of France and Germany combined.

Colleagues and I studied more than 2,100 potential Australian tourists following the disaster. They were uncertain whether a visit would help, though many were willing to travel to support recovery.

An important lesson from that and other research is that the tourism consequences of a disaster do not necessarily follow its geographical boundaries.

It has shown that if you’re trying to get tourists to return sooner, as Nepal is already doing, you’re better to appeal to people who’ve visited a region several times before, as they’re more likely to return than less frequent visitors.

That matters when thinking about how Nepal’s tourism can recover. But this does not mean Nepal should try to bring tourists back as quickly as possible.

Timing and trusted information

Reopening too soon can put visitors at risk and strain resources needed by affected communities.

Traveller confidence needs to be earned through credible and detailed information to provide reassurance.

As recovery progresses, travellers wanting to visit Nepal will need to know:

which specific places remain affected

which roads and trekking routes are accessible

what infrastructure is operating

and where authorities continue to advise against travel.

Nepal is already working hard to get some of these travel updates out to the world, including through social media posts tagged with #NepalCalling.

Our research following Cyclone Marcia in Queensland similarly found that trust and consistent communication between tourism organisations were critical to effective recovery.

The objective is to manage the return of tourism in a way that supports affected communities, without putting visitors or residents at greater risk.

People visiting friends and relatives in Nepal, or other tourists who have visited the country before, are the most likely to return earlier once Nepal is ready, due to their stronger personal ties and better knowledge of local conditions.

The challenge for Nepal is not simply deciding when the country is “open” again. It is being clear about which specific places are ready for visitors to return, and when tourism will support Nepalese communities – not complicate their recovery.

Travellers should also check their own government’s official travel advice, such as Australia’s Smart Traveller, New Zealand’s Smart Travel and the United States’ State Department websites.

About the author Professor Brent Ritchie is a Professor of Tourism Management at The University of Queensland. His research focuses on tourism risk management and understanding risk from an individual and organisational perspective.

title: Climate Change Primed Nepal Glacier for Deadly Collapse, Attribution Study Finds - theenergymix.com
description: Climate Change Primed Nepal Glacier for Deadly Collapse, Attribution Study Finds  theenergymix.com
publisher.title: theenergymix.com
full_article:
Climate attribution researchers say “there is absolutely no doubt” that decades of global warming set the stage for the deadly rock and glacier collapse on Langtang Lirung Mountain in Nepal, Inside Climate News reports.

At least 1,300 people died in August when a cascade of semi-frozen sludge, boulders, trees, and other debris roared through the region at speeds up to 100 mph and crested up to 300 feet high, Inside Climate writes. The disaster destroyed and damaged towns, farms, orchards, roads, bridges, and energy infrastructure, devastating livelihoods across the region. The total losses are now estimated at about US$5 billion.

In a new analysis of the Aug. 26 disaster, a team of scientists with World Weather Attribution highlighted that record-hot temperatures baked the region in the months before the disaster. That was preceded by unusually high snowfall in late 2025, which is usually a very dry time for the region. Additional meltwater from the snow was probably another element in a complex chain of climate-linked factors contributing to the disaster, said Walter Immerzeel, a co-author of the new analysis.

Warming has hollowed out ancient ice and thawed the permafrost, the frozen ground that helps bind high mountain slopes together, leaving them increasingly vulnerable to collapse.

Get the latest climate news and analysis, direct to your inbox. Subscribe Today View our latest digests

According to new estimates, about 116 million cubic metres of rock and ice initially broke away from the face of the mountain, the equivalent of a 96-square-block area of Manhattan breaking off all at once and plunging several thousand vertical feet within minutes. The size of the initial disintegration is unprecedented in the Himalayas, said Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands who spent years researching in the region affected by the recent catastrophe.

The volume is about five times that of the most comparable mountain collapse and flood in the region, the 2021 Chamoli disaster in Uttarakhand, India. The increasing frequency and scale of mountain and glacier collapses and subsequent floods are signs of “fundamental, irreversible shifts in Himalayan mountain environments,” Immerzeel said.

Nepal has sought aid from the international fund for climate losses and damage set up through the United Nations climate framework. But the fund only has about $800 million pledged, with roughly $350 million available for claims, a fraction of the estimated damage from this single disaster.

The flood first swept through the upper Lhende valley and the settlements of Rasuwa district, including Rasuwagadhi and Timure, before surging through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, about 100 miles downstream. About 5,000 people are still missing.

Immerzeel said the new analysis highlights the changes in background conditions that affect hazards for people and resources. That may be more consequential than identifying the exact trigger for a single specific event, several co-authors said during a media briefing on the new analysis.

Immerzeel said climate change from burning fossil fuels is pushing the freezing line upward by roughly 100 metres per decade, heating bedrock that has been frozen in place for thousands of years and spreading that heat beneath the glaciers.

Some of the melting ice has been frozen for tens of thousands of years. Warm meltwater flows deep into cracks in the rocks, exerting enormous hydraulic pressure. Then it refreezes in winter, widening the fissures; when it melts again in spring, gravity takes hold.

“When you combine high-elevation permafrost degradation with glacier retreat and record summer heat, the structural integrity of these mountain walls is compromised,” Immerzeel said. “The catastrophic impacts of what can then happen are clear for all to see.”

Co-author Prof. Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London, said the analysis shows how permafrost thawing, glacier thinning, and more rain instead of snow had the effect of “preconditioning” the mountain for collapse.

She said scientists could be even more specific about how much human-caused warming contributed to the disaster with more detailed glacier modelling and readings from nearby glaciers. But that shouldn’t matter in the context of funding to cover the cost of climate impacts, she added, addressing the question of who should help Nepal pay for a climate disaster caused by billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions from rich, developed countries.

Co-author Madhab Uprety, a technical expert with the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said the extreme flood challenged basic assumptions about what communities in the region must prepare for.

title: A Crisis in Images: The Influx of AI Generated Imagery on the Nepal Flood May Reinvigorate Journalism’s Watchdog Role. - Monash Lens
description: A Crisis in Images: The Influx of AI Generated Imagery on the Nepal Flood May Reinvigorate Journalism’s Watchdog Role.  Monash Lens
publisher.title: Monash Lens
full_article:
On the morning of 26 August 2026, the first indication of the scope of the crisis unfolding in Nepal came from CCTV footage showing the Rasuwagadhi border point being inundated with a tsunami-like wall of water and mud. This raw video was quickly followed by images of the widespread devastation, and burgeoning rescue efforts, images captured by Nepal-based visual journalists, including Associated Press (AP) photographer, Niranjan Shrestha and Reuters’ Navesh Chitrakar . Their documentation served as a reminder of the power of the image to capture the human condition in times of crisis.

Within hours of the first verified images of the unfolding disaster in Nepal emerging, an influx of AI generated imagery (stills and video) appeared on social media feeds. Media outlets such as Australian Associated Press (AAP), ABC , France 24 and BBC published articles and videos on these fake images providing audiences with tips on how to identify fabrications. Some fake posts featured footage from past disasters, such as a video posted on X which was from a 2025 mudslide in India . Another Facebook post, which AAP ran through a Google reverse image search, was from a flood in Japan in 2021. This post was viewed more than 360,000 times. It is common to use old recycled footage to spread misinformation, with past imagery from Chile, India and Alaska used to illustrate the Nepal crisis. AI images of missing persons were also posted . France 24 reported on multiple fake videos including one that was viewed seven million times on X.

AAP flagged the image pictured below (Figure 1) as AI generated. I also tested this image with AI detection software Sightengine, which reported a score of 99 per cent AI generated. The same AI image (Figures 1 & 2) was used on more than one Facebook feed in different contexts and liked and shared multiple times. Facebook did not flag this as AI content whereas it did flag Figures 3 and 4 as AI content. Given that Facebook can mislabel images, I also ran these images through Sightengine and it confirmed these images were AI generated. However, the accompanying text suggests otherwise: “this is what resilience looks like.”

Figure 1: posted on Facebook August 27, 7:29pm

Figure 2: posted on Facebook August 27, 8:34pm

Figure 3: Facebook labelled this AI content

Figure 4: Facebook labelled this AI content

In Nepal, the Press Council launched a new site, “Special Complaints on the Bhotekoshi Incident" , to enable people to report fake imagery and other forms of misinformation. In its first day of operation, more than 100 complaints were made and the Council instructed 72 social media users to take down content .

The verification and fact checking practices that media have applied to Nepal flood imagery act to both maintain the credibility of news sources, and to reassert the value of journalism at a time when it is contested. Fact checking and verification are fundamental journalistic practices. Traditionally conducted in-house, in 2016 these practices became more prominent in the “post truth” era, when attacks on journalism as fake news escalated.

Why does it matter if there are fake images and videos circulating? Visuals are often the first point of entry into a story and can shape the way audiences respond. In the Age of the Image we are acculturated to receive our news in pictures, both still and moving images. Seeing is believing is embedded in our DNA, our first instinct to accept that what we are looking at is real. Reading photographs is considered “relatively automatic and cognitively cost free” and in the digital media landscape, the consumption of imagery is conducted at a rapid pace. Attention spans on digital devices have declined from 75 seconds in 2012 to 47 seconds in 2024 leaving little time for critical analysis. An inability to sustain attention combined with the rise of easily accessible AI tools that flood feeds with fake content, distracts from the reality of the situation compromising issue salience. It also means that few people verify the information they consume, like and share.

Fake content can amplify panic and distress amongst affected communities. It can impact rescue services and emergency aid. And it can undermine the charity sector by seeding doubt about what are genuine and fake calls for donations. Fake visuals also contribute to the erosion of trust in visual journalism and the important, and often dangerous, work these professionals do.

title: Opinion | Why Nepal’s youth-led government inherited the toughest job in Asia - kathmandupost.com
description: Opinion | Why Nepal’s youth-led government inherited the toughest job in Asia  kathmandupost.com
publisher.title: kathmandupost.com
full_article:
Nepal continues to occupy one of the most strategically sensitive geopolitical spaces in Asia, wedged between two nuclear powers who watch its domestic politics with keen interest. The country contributes around 0.1 percent to the global greenhouse gas emissions. These two facts rarely appear in the same sentence, but they should.

A country that pollutes insignificantly is now paying for a warming planet with landslides and glacial floods. It is the same country that controls almost none of its own regional strategic weather, yet is expected to hold an even keel between Beijing and New Delhi. The world watches as a small, landlocked, mountainous state attempts to survive being squeezed from two fronts at once: by emerging powers on one front and a changing climate on the other.

Nepal has no coastline, no navy, and no industrial base capable of independent leverage in the geopolitical equation. What it has instead is its position as a narrow corridor separating the Indian plains from the Tibetan plateau. For most of its modern history, this position functioned as a form of protection. The country has survived by being useful to both sides and threatening to neither. That arrangement is now under strain.

China’s interest in Nepal has hardened beyond diplomatic courtesy. Stability on the Tibetan frontier, adherence to the One-China policy, and the steady extension of Belt and Road infrastructure sit at the centre of Beijing’s calculations. India’s stake is older and denser: an open border, shared religious and cultural life, deep economic dependence, and a direct interest in how Kathmandu manages water, connectivity and security along a frontier that touches its own restive north. Neither relationship can replace the other, and neither can be safely ignored. That is the uncomfortable arithmetic Nepal’s leaders inherit, whatever mandate they carry at home.

This political test arrives at the precise moment Nepal’s political order has been upended. Years and decades of public anger at corruption, nepotism and institutional drift culminated in youth-led protests in September 2025 that swept aside much of the old political establishment and put a new, largely untested generation of leaders into government.

That change was overwhelmingly domestic in character, driven by frustration with governance failures at home. However, new governments do not get to choose which inheritances they take on. Whoever now sits in Kathmandu’s ministries inherits the same narrow corridor between Beijing and New Delhi, the same fragile glaciers, and the same thin margin for error that every predecessor faced, minus the experience of having managed either pressure before.

Here is the point worth dwelling on, because it is where most commentary goes soft: Competition between regional powers is not automatically bad for the smaller state caught between them. Rival interests can mean rival investment, rival infrastructure offers, rival willingness to overlook Kathmandu’s domestic failings in exchange for goodwill. The danger lies in the loss of manoeuvring room that comes from tilting too far towards either one. A Nepal seen in Beijing as an Indian client state reduces Chinese engagement. A Nepal seen in New Delhi as a platform for Chinese security interests damages the depth of an irreplaceable relationship. Strategic autonomy, in this context, is a survival technique, and it must be practised daily.

This is where new, inexperienced political leadership is most exposed. Populist mandates require decisiveness. Hedging looks, to an impatient electorate, like indecision or worse, like weakness dressed up as diplomacy. A newly empowered government under pressure to demonstrate results may be tempted to lean visibly towards one neighbour to extract a quick infrastructure win or a headline-grabbing loan. That temptation should be resisted, not because balance is elegant in theory, but because the cost of overcorrection is not abstract. Border sensitivities, territorial disputes and infrastructure disagreements between Nepal and its neighbours have flared before over far smaller provocations than a visible strategic tilt. Nationalist posturing plays well domestically and rarely produces anything durable.

If the India-China balancing act is the pressure Nepal faces from its flanks, climate change is the pressure arriving from above, and it is arguably the less forgiving of the two. Diplomacy can be recalibrated. A collapsing glacial lake cannot be renegotiated. The recent floods and mudslides in Nepal, the disaster some have called the ‘Himalayan Tsunami’, were the visible edge of a broader pattern: The Himalayan region is warming faster than the global average, glacial instability is accelerating, and mountain hydrology that took centuries to stabilise is being rewritten within a single generation. Nepal did almost nothing to cause this. It is nonetheless first in line to absorb the consequences.

This is where the word injustice earns its place rather than serving as rhetorical decoration. The industrialised economies that built their prosperity on two centuries of fossil fuel consumption are not the ones whose villages are being swept away. The states with the least capacity to adapt, the fewest resources to rebuild, and the smallest contribution to the problem are absorbing the worst of it. That asymmetry is precisely what the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, written into the climate treaty architecture decades ago, was meant to address. It has not been enough, and Nepal’s catastrophes are the latest evidence of that failure.

There is, however, a shift worth taking seriously. The International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of July 2025 confirmed that states carry binding obligations under international law to prevent significant climate harm, to cooperate on impacts, and to protect human rights threatened by a warming planet, and that states responsible for that harm may face legal consequences, including claims for reparation. This does not hand Nepal a cheque. It hands Nepal something more useful in the medium term: a legal vocabulary. Loss and damage funding, framed as an entitlement grounded in prevention of transboundary harm, the polluter pays principle and international human rights law, is a fundamentally different diplomatic instrument than an appeal for charity. Nepal’s approach to the UN’s Loss and Damage Fund following the recent disaster should be read in that light, as the opening move in a longer legal and political campaign rather than a one-off request.

The two pressures, geopolitical and climatic, are not separate problems requiring separate strategies. They intersect directly over the one resource Nepal actually possesses in abundance: hydropower. Vast, largely untapped hydroelectric potential is simultaneously Nepal’s best economic asset and the terrain on which Indian and Chinese interests will compete hardest, given both neighbours’ appetite for cross-border transmission and regional energy cooperation. Managed well, hydropower could fund the very adaptation and resilience measures that climate vulnerability demands, turning geography from liability into leverage. Managed carelessly, under pressure to strike a fast deal with one side, it becomes another arena of dependency dressed up as development.

title: Floods in Nepal disrupt schooling for more than 14,500 children — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Floods in Nepal disrupt schooling for more than 14,500 children — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, floods on the Bhotekoshi River disrupted schooling for more than 14,500 children in 63 educational institutions in the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. A total of 9,430 students were directly affected, including those who lost their parents, homes or schools, Kathmandu Post reports, citing an assessment by the country’s Ministry of Education.

Schooling for thousands of other children is being delayed because school buildings are being used as temporary shelters for displaced residents. In 28 of the 29 such centers in the three districts, people are living in school buildings; 22 centers operate in Nuwakot and another six in Rasuwa. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, around 2,000 people are staying in these centers.

Damaged schools and missing students

According to the authorities, following the August 26 floods caused by a glacier collapse, the bodies of 1,409 victims were found. Another 4,089 people are considered missing. The Ministry of Education said that at least 100 children lost both parents, while nearly 500 students enrolled in schools are still considered missing. A total of 1,372 students were displaced by the disaster.

The floods physically damaged 34 educational institutions: 45 buildings containing 268 classrooms were affected. Eleven schools completely ceased operations due to destruction or safety threats, while another four are temporarily closed. The disaster also destroyed 82 toilets and water supply systems, 20 other water sources, 3,232 textbooks, 2,227 sets of learning materials, 4,561 desks and benches, 194 computers and 144 laptops.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot sustained the greatest losses, with more than 3,000 students affected. The assessment records 227 missing schoolchildren and 11 teachers there. Nepal Rastriya Basic School in Timure was destroyed: of its 35 students, 25 are still considered missing, as are six of its 11 teachers.

Temporary classrooms and accommodation for children

The Ministry of Education plans to establish 68 temporary learning centers at destroyed schools. Thirteen such centers have already opened, each designed for 30 students. The authorities are also distributing learning materials, organizing psychosocial support and resuming classes at schools that did not sustain significant damage and are not being used as shelters.

The government is preparing dormitory accommodation for children who lost their parents, cannot reach schools because of destroyed roads and bridges, or live far from functioning educational institutions. The Bagmati provincial authorities plan to accommodate 200 students at Chhetratrapal Secondary School in Likhu, while Uttargaya Rural Municipality plans to place another 250 students at Nilkantha Secondary School. The ministry also announced the creation of a Scholarship Bank fund to provide affected children with full and partial scholarships, including accommodation support.

title: Nepal sees more severe Japanese encephalitis cases among adults - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal sees more severe Japanese encephalitis cases among adults  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Since June, Nepal has recorded 121 cases of Japanese encephalitis, 26 of which ended in death. The case fatality rate is 21.5%, the highest among vector-borne diseases in the country, Kathmandu Post reports, citing Health Ministry data.

Officials expect infections to increase further as the peak disease season continues. This year, Japanese encephalitis cases have been detected in 84 local units across 36 districts in all seven provinces of the country.

Unvaccinated adults at risk

Specialists note a shift in the age structure of cases. Previously, children were the main group to become severely ill and die, but severe cases and deaths are now increasingly recorded among people over 30. Most people in this age group have not received a Japanese encephalitis vaccination.

According to government officials, 77% of deaths occurred among people over 50, and none of those who died had been vaccinated. The highest number of deaths — at least six — was recorded in Jhapa District. Two deaths each were registered in Sunsari, Saptari, Parsa, Kailali and Arghakhanchi districts.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

In 2022, at least four of 79 infected people died from Japanese encephalitis; in 2023, 20 of 108 died; in 2024, 28 of 86 died; and in 2025, 41 of 183 died. The highest case fatality rate was recorded in 2024, at 33%.

Vaccination campaigns

Nepal began vaccinating against Japanese encephalitis in 2006, and since 2015 the vaccine has been included in the routine program and is available free of charge at state medical facilities. However, the program does not cover adults, although many severe cases have been recorded among them in recent years.

The Health Ministry has completed preparations to vaccinate people over 30 in three local units of Kailali District: Dhangadhi, Lamkichuha and Ghodaghodi. Vaccination across Jhapa District is planned to begin on September 21. At the same time, the government has not allocated funds this year to vaccinate the entire unvaccinated population.

Japanese encephalitis is transmitted through bites from infected Culex mosquitoes, which breed, among other places, in rice fields. Pigs and ducks are natural reservoirs of the virus. There is no specific treatment for the disease: medical care is aimed at controlling symptoms and complications. According to the World Health Organization, about one-third of people with severe disease die, while up to half of survivors may have severe lifelong impairments.

full_article:
In Nepal, a new generation of political leaders that came to power after youth protests in September 2025 must simultaneously maintain a balance in relations with China and India and respond to the consequences of climate change. This is reported by Kathmandu Post.

According to the publication, years of public outrage over corruption, nepotism and the degradation of institutions led to protests that pushed aside a significant part of the old political establishment. At the same time, the new, largely inexperienced authorities inherited the geopolitical and climate challenges faced by their predecessors.

Balance between two neighbors

Nepal is located between India and China, two nuclear-armed states that closely monitor the country’s domestic politics. Beijing’s interests are linked to stability along the Tibetan border, the one-China policy and infrastructure development under the Belt and Road Initiative. For India, the open border, economic ties, water resources, transport links and security are important.

The publication notes that competition between China and India may create opportunities for Nepal for investment and infrastructure projects. However, excessive rapprochement with one of the neighbors could limit room for maneuver in relations with the other. The new authorities may be particularly vulnerable under pressure from expectations of rapid economic results.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Climate losses and hydropower

Nepal’s share of global greenhouse gas emissions is about 0.1%, but the country suffers from landslides, floods and glacier instability. Kathmandu Post notes that the Himalayan region is warming faster than the global average, while changes in glaciers are altering mountain hydrology.

In July 2025, the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion, confirmed states’ obligations to prevent significant climate harm, cooperate on its consequences and protect human rights threatened by warming. The publication believes this could give Nepal additional legal arguments in appeals for loss and damage funding.

One of the country’s key resources remains its considerable but largely untapped hydropower potential. It could become a source of funds for adaptation to climate change, but it is also an area of competition between Indian and Chinese interests due to the development of cross-border energy grids.

full_article:
In Nepal, the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) received 40,542 complaints about possible violations in the 2025–2026 fiscal year. The conviction rate in cases heard by the Special Court fell to 51.92%, compared with 52.67% a year earlier and 65.24% in the 2023–2024 fiscal year, Kathmandu Post reports.

During the year, the CIAA filed 156 cases with the Special Court, and in 81 of them the court upheld the charges brought by the commission. The commission also appealed 104 Special Court decisions to the Supreme Court and filed three review petitions. The CIAA investigates, among other things, cases involving corruption, illicit enrichment, forged academic certificates and bribery.

Claims worth 5.24 billion rupees

In cases filed during the fiscal year, the commission sought compensation for damages amounting to 5.24 billion Nepalese rupees. They involved 990 defendants: 145 women, 801 men and 44 organisations. The largest number of cases — 56 — concerned the loss or improper use of public property.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Former CIAA chief commissioner Suryanath Upadhyay said the lower rate indicates a need to strengthen investigations and collect evidence more thoroughly before filing cases in court. Public administration researcher Dipesh Ghimire linked the result to the commission’s expertise, investigative methods and the capacity of its investigators. According to him, some cases may have reached court without sufficiently thorough investigations.

Complaints against local and federal authorities

In the previous fiscal year, the CIAA received 37,026 complaints. The largest number of complaints concerned local authorities — 20,025. Among the ten local units with the highest number of complaints, Kathmandu Metropolitan City ranked first, with 441 complaints filed against it.

Among federal bodies, the largest number of complaints — 3,036 — concerned the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration. This accounted for more than 19% of the 15,512 complaints registered against federal government institutions during the year.

full_article:
In Nepal, around 40 officials and members of the former central working committee of the Nepali Congress who had remained in the faction of former party president Sher Bahadur Deuba have joined the camp of the current party leader, Gagan Thapa. The politicians arrived at the party’s central office in Sanepa to take part in preparations for the general convention, Kathmandu Post reports.

Dialogue instead of a split

Purna Bahadur Khadka, who had previously served as acting party president, played an important role in the transition of Deuba’s allies. He refused to lead a possible split in the Nepali Congress and began negotiations with Thapa. After that, a significant number of politicians, including figures close to Deuba, supported Khadka.

At a party meeting on October 14 last year, Deuba announced a break from active politics and transferred the powers of acting president to Khadka. At the same time, according to the publication, Khadka did not have the full trust of Deuba’s closest circle. There were also suspicions within the party that he was close to Thapa and Bishwo Prakash Sharma.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Agreement on participation in the convention

On April 17, the Supreme Court recognized the special general convention and Thapa’s election as party president as legitimate. After that, representatives of Deuba’s faction raised the issue of including in the central working committee 111 officials and members of the body’s former composition who had not joined it after the special convention.

Thapa said he was ready to consider proposals from Khadka and another party leader, Shekhar Koirala. Later, the sides agreed to allow members who had reinstated but not renewed their active membership to attend the convention, include representatives of Deuba’s former leadership in the central working committee, and involve all factions in committees and structures related to holding the convention.

Thapa also said that he wants to invite Deuba as the chief guest to the convention’s opening ceremony and will continue efforts to involve him in the event.

full_article:
Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, during a visit to New Delhi, India, asked for support for the reconstruction of property and infrastructure destroyed by floods in the Bhotekoshi area. At a meeting with India’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, he said that Nepal was counting on substantial assistance for reconstruction.

As the Kathmandu Post reports, Wagle requested a grant but did not name a specific amount. Sitharaman replied that India would assess Nepal’s needs after the post-disaster needs assessment is completed and would then determine the amount of support.

Damage assessment and reconstruction

Nepalese authorities have instructed that the scale of flood damage be assessed; the final report is expected within four weeks. A committee established by the government is to determine reconstruction and rehabilitation needs in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, which were affected the most.

After the assessment is completed, Nepal plans either to convene a donors’ conference or seek assistance from friendly states, the donor community, and charitable organizations. Aid is also planned to be directed toward creating climate-resilient infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi River.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Loans after the 2015 earthquake

The sides also discussed negotiations on a line of credit that India offered Nepal about ten years ago. After the 2015 earthquake, New Delhi announced a package of 100 billion Indian rupees: 25 billion rupees as a grant and 75 billion rupees as a concessional loan through the Export-Import Bank of India.

According to the publication, Nepal was unable to use the credit portion because of conditions set by the Indian side. In May, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal proposed directing these concessional funds to the energy sector. He also proposed that India provide $500 million in grants and another $500 million in concessional loans for infrastructure, including roads and energy, but this proposal is being reconsidered after the floods.

India’s Ministry of Finance said the talks concerned strengthening economic ties, trade, investment, and transport connectivity. Nepal’s Embassy in New Delhi also noted that the sides discussed energy. Sitharaman expressed condolences over the deaths caused by the floods and assured continued support for Nepal’s recovery.

title: Warming, 2015 quake 'behind Nepal disaster' after scientists trace glacier thaw - Telegraph India
description: Warming, 2015 quake 'behind Nepal disaster' after scientists trace glacier thaw  Telegraph India

full_article:
Climatic drivers, especially warming, piggybacking on geological factors, played a key role in triggering the August 26 avalanche that devastated Nepal, according to a rapid scientific analysis released this week by World Weather Attribution scientists and international glaciologists.

Earlier, some researchers had said it was difficult to conclusively link a fast-moving, localised rock-ice avalanche to global warming. The massive rock-and-ice collapse on the country's northern border swept away communities and localities.

"Scientists identify the role of climate change on possible causal factors of the collapse, which resulted in devastation well in excess of adaptation limits," reads the report. World Weather Attribution is an international scientific collaboration that analyses and communicates the possible influence of climate change on extreme weather events, such as storms, extreme rainfall, heatwaves and droughts.

"Decades of atmospheric warming — caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels — have melted the glacier and pushed the freezing threshold line (0°C isotherm) upward by around 100 metres of altitude per decade," states the report, explaining that "…this has resulted in glacier recession and thawing occurring in permafrost within rock fractures that historically hold high mountain walls together, rendering them unstable". The report adds that the 2015 earthquake of 7.8 magnitude is likely to have preconditioned the slope for collapse.

"The fingerprints of climate change are clear to see in long-term changes…. We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse. This increases the risk in a region that is already exposed to high seismic activity," said Ben Clarke, an extreme weather and climate change researcher from Imperial College London and a member of the research team.

Apart from glacial thinning, permafrost thaw and compound preconditioning because of the massive earthquake in 2015, high locally recorded recent temperatures and increased meltwater were identified as major causes behind the sudden flood that ravaged the area and its people, at a speed of more than 190km per hour in the initial flow, the report suggests.

"July and August 2026 — directly before the collapse — were the warmest on record locally. High snowfall in October and November 2025 added large amounts of meltwater in the months preceding the collapse," the report says.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, said: "The science is now unambiguous: fossil-fuelled warming thinned the glaciers and thawed the permafrost that held the mountain together. Nepal did nothing to cause this, yet its people are paying with their lives. This is climate injustice — and the Loss and Damage Fund must deliver now, not as charity, but as compensation and reparations." Nepal has urged the Loss and Damage Fund for financial support.

The Fill the Fund campaign is a global climate initiative demanding that wealthy nations and corporate polluters fully finance the United Nations "Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage".

"The Bhote Koshi catastrophe is a stark warning of the growing risks people are facing with the rapidly warming Himalaya," added Manjeet Dhakal, director of climate analytics South Asia.

title: Nepal’s court suspends two House of Representatives rules — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal’s court suspends two House of Representatives rules — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS

full_article:
Nepal’s Supreme Court has temporarily suspended the application of two provisions of the House of Representatives Rules of Procedure — Rules 140(11) and 259. The interim order concerns provisions adopted by the lower house of parliament on May 31.

Contested provisions

As Kathmandu Post reports in an editorial, Rule 140(11) provided for the possibility of certifying bills on constitutional amendments through a combined vote of the two houses of parliament by a two-thirds majority.

According to the publication, this could have made it easier for the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party to introduce constitutional amendments. The party holds nearly two-thirds of the seats in the House of Representatives but does not have a single seat in the National Assembly. The publication believes that, with the support of several allied parties, the RSP could have secured the required combined majority in the two houses.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Rule 259 granted the Rules of Procedure the status of a special federal law. In Kathmandu Post’s view, this could have placed the Rules of Procedure above other legislative acts and potentially put members of the lower house beyond the reach of the law.

Editorial position

The article states that in a bicameral parliamentary system, both houses bear shared responsibility for lawmaking. The editorial emphasizes that the adoption by one house of rules granting it extraordinary powers runs counter to constitutional and democratic principles.

Kathmandu Post called on the Rastriya Swatantra Party to bring the contested provisions into line with the Constitution and begin a broad discussion of the issue in the House of Representatives. The Supreme Court has not yet issued a final ruling in the case.
